title: A Clock That Ticks Inside an Atom's Core Could Unlock New Physics
summary: For over 15 years, Thorsten Schumm chased what many considered a wild dream: building a clock that ticks not by the jump of an atom's electrons, but by the jump of its nucleus. Now, that dream is reality. In a landmark experiment, Schumm's team at the Vienna University of Technology and collaborators have demonstrated the first continuously operating nuclear clock. The device uses a rare isotope, thorium-229, whose nucleus has an unusually low-energy excited state that can be triggered by ultraviolet laser light. By locking a laser to that nuclear transition, the researchers created a timekeeper that ran for 24 hours straight — a crucial step toward practical applications. "Having worked in this field for more than 15 years, it is just beautiful, how a very 'wild' idea such as manipulating an atomic nucleus with a laser has turned into reality," Schumm told Live Science. Nuclear clocks promise to surpass even today's best optical atomic clocks, which would lose less than a second over 100 million years. Because the nucleus is shielded by its electron cloud, it's 1,000 to 10,000 times less sensitive to environmental noise like electric or magnetic fields. That inherent stability could lead to clocks that are not only more precise but also more robust. Unlike many atomic clocks that require ultracold atoms suspended in a vacuum chamber, the thorium nuclei are embedded in a crystal at room temperature. This solid-state design could eventually yield compact, portable clocks for navigation, telecommunications, and data synchronization. But for many physicists, the real thrill lies in fundamental physics. Atomic clocks primarily probe electromagnetic interactions. A nuclear clock, however, is sensitive to the strong nuclear force and the weak force — two of the universe's four fundamental forces. This makes it a potential detector for phenomena beyond the Standard Model. "Essentially all modern theories beyond the standard model predict additional particles or 5th forces," Schumm explained. "These can be probed with the nuclear clock in some parameter regime." In other words, this tiny ticking nucleus could help answer some of the biggest questions in physics — from the nature of dark matter to the existence of a fifth fundamental force. The road to this breakthrough was long. Researchers spent years identifying the exact laser frequency needed to excite thorium-229, and the development of continuous-wave lasers was key. Before that, they had to excite the nucleus and then wait minutes for it to decay — far too slow for a practical clock. "With the continuous lasers, we can measure the nucleus in absorption and get an immediate response," Schumm said. "Once we had that, it was 'just' implementing some electronics and atomization to have the clock stabilize itself to the nucleus." The team's next steps will focus on improving the clock's precision and stability, but the first tick has already echoed through the physics world.
why_it_matters: This experiment demonstrates that chasing seemingly 'wild' ideas about tiny atomic particles can lead to tools that answer gigantic questions about dark matter and the fundamental laws of nature. For students, it's a reminder that curiosity-driven science — not just practical inventions — often sparks the most world-changing discoveries, and that persistence over many years can pay off in surprising ways.

background_read: For centuries, humans have built ever more accurate clocks — from sundials to mechanical clocks, then quartz, and later atomic clocks. The best optical atomic clocks today would lose less than one second over 100 million years, working by measuring the vibrations of electrons as they jump between energy levels in atoms like strontium or ytterbium.

A nuclear clock, however, uses the atom's incredibly dense core (the nucleus) instead of its electrons. Because the nucleus is shielded by its surrounding electron cloud, it's much less disturbed by magnetic or electric fields — making it inherently more stable. The catch has always been that most nuclei need ultra-high-energy rays to change states, not a controllable laser.

Thorium-229 is the one known exception: its nucleus has an excited state of unusually low energy, allowing it to be triggered by ultraviolet laser light. Thorsten Schumm, a physicist at the Vienna University of Technology, and his collaborators spent more than 15 years finding the exact laser frequency and developing the necessary continuous-wave lasers to keep the clock ticking steadily.

Such a clock isn't just a better timekeeper. It is sensitive to the strong nuclear force and the weak force — two of the four fundamental forces of the universe. Any tiny deviation in its tick could be a sign of dark matter particles or a mysterious fifth force, both of which lie beyond the Standard Model of particle physics that currently explains our universe.

perspectives.description: Proponents see a future where portable nuclear clocks revolutionize GPS, internet synchronization, and deep-space navigation. Moreover, the ability to probe new physics beyond the Standard Model could lead to breakthroughs as big as the discovery of the Higgs boson.

Skeptics note that optical atomic clocks are already staggeringly accurate, and a nuclear clock’s marginal improvement might not justify the huge investment and complexity. Practical applications could be decades away, and no one can guarantee the experiments will actually find dark matter or new forces.

Historically, the pursuit of ever-better clocks has repeatedly unlocked new discoveries — from testing Einstein’s relativity to developing the GPS we use today. A nuclear clock is a natural next step in metrology, driven by the simple principle that observing nature more precisely often reveals hidden patterns.

If the stability can be improved, a nuclear clock in space could one day detect gravitational waves in a frequency range inaccessible to current detectors. Even more intriguing, a confirmed fifth force would force physicists to rewrite textbooks, potentially altering our understanding of everything from galaxy formation to the ultimate fate of the universe.
